---
title: "Labor Productivity"
---

```{R}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
devtools::load_all()
library(tidyverse)
library(zoo)
library(psych)
library(kableExtra)
```

The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) publishes quarterly labor productivity growth rates (% change from previous quarter) for major US economic sectors. We analyze five sectors:

- `DUR`: Durable manufacturing
- `NDUR`: Nondurable manufacturing
- `NFC`: Nonfinancial corporate
- `NFBUS`: Nonfarm business
- `BUS`: Business

Productivity growth is subject to structural breaks driven by recessions, policy changes, and technological shifts — making this a natural setting for ECE. We compare ECE against oracle segmentation, where change points are estimated from the data using `segment_mean()`. `NFBUS` and `BUS` are both broad aggregates covering most of the economy, so we expect them to move together; the other three sectors are more loosely related components of the same business cycle.

```{R labor-load-data}
#| echo: false
#| message: false

X_data <- read_csv(
  "~/Documents/Research/Code/ECE/data/real-data/bls-labor-productivity.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

# Reconstruct quarterly dates starting 1987 Q2
n <- nrow(X_data)
dates <- as.yearqtr("1987 Q2") + (0:(n - 1)) / 4

X_mat     <- as.matrix(X_data)
X_segment <- segment_mean(X_mat, penalty = "Manual", pen.value = 0) |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  rename_with(~ paste0(.x, "_segment"))
X_seg_mat <- as.matrix(X_segment)
X_resid   <- X_mat - X_seg_mat

X <- bind_cols(date = dates, X_data, X_segment)
```

## Diagnostics

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Plot

```{R labor-plot-raw}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-bls-productivity
#| fig-cap: "Quarterly labor productivity growth by sector. Thick lines show segmented means."

X |>
  pivot_longer(cols = -date, names_to = "series", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(
    type   = if_else(str_ends(series, "_segment"), "Segmented", "Raw"),
    sector = str_remove(series, "_segment$")
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = date, y = value, color = sector, group = series)) +
  geom_line(aes(linewidth = type)) +
  scale_linewidth_manual(values = c(Raw = 0.5, Segmented = 1.0), guide = "none") +
  labs(
    title = "Labor Productivity by Sector",
    x = "Date",
    y = "% Change from Previous Quarter",
    color = "Sector",
    caption = "Source: Bureau of Labor Statistics"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Residuals

```{R labor-plot-residuals}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-bls-residuals
#| fig-cap: "Residuals after removing the segmented mean from each sector."

X_resid |>
  as_tibble() |>
  bind_cols(date = dates) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = -date, names_to = "sector", values_to = "value") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = date, y = value, color = sector)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "gray") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~sector, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    title = "Residuals after Segmentation",
    x = "Date",
    y = "Residual",
    color = "Sector"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

### Mean-Shift-Invariant

Same ECE-term grammar as `plot_ece_terms()` (raw pairwise term in gray, rolling mean in blue, dashed global mean), but laid out as the upper triangle of a pxp matrix so each panel's row/column position matches its place in the correlation matrix above.

```{R labor-trend-ece}
#| echo: false

window <- max(10, floor(nrow(X_mat) / 5))
cn     <- colnames(X_mat)
idx    <- combn(ncol(X_mat), 2)

ece_terms_tri <- purrr::map_dfr(seq_len(ncol(idx)), function(k) {
  i <- idx[1, k]
  j <- idx[2, k]
  s <- lag_term(X_mat[, i], X_mat[, j])
  tibble(
    t = seq_len(nrow(X_mat)), row = cn[i], col = cn[j],
    raw = s, run = rolling_mean(s, window), global = mean(s)
  )
}) |>
  mutate(
    row = factor(row, levels = cn[1:(ncol(X_mat) - 1)]),
    col = factor(col, levels = cn[2:ncol(X_mat)])
  )

ggplot(ece_terms_tri, aes(x = t)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = raw), color = "gray80") +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = global), linetype = "dashed", color = "firebrick") +
  geom_line(aes(y = run), color = "steelblue", na.rm = TRUE) +
  facet_grid(rows = vars(row), cols = vars(col), scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "time", y = "ECE term (covariance scale)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Correlation

```{R labor-calc-cor}
#| echo: false

ece_cor         <- ece.cor(X_mat) |> round(3)
rownames(ece_cor) <- colnames(ece_cor) <- colnames(X_data)

segment_cor     <- cor(X_resid) |> round(3)
pearson_cor     <- cor(X_mat) |> round(3)

ece_pmat        <- ece_pval(X_mat) |> round(3)
segment_pmat    <- cor_pval(X_resid) |> round(3)
pearson_pmat    <- cor_pval(X_mat) |> round(3)
```

## Results

Beyond the pairwise correlations above, we can test the joint null hypothesis that the full 5x5 correlation matrix is diagonal — i.e. that none of the five sectors are contemporaneously correlated.

```{R labor-diagonal-tests}
#| echo: false
set.seed(123)

results <- data.frame(
  Method = c(
    "Bootstrap Multiplier",
    "Parametric Bootstrap",
    "Parametric Bootstrap (Naive)",
    "Bartlett Test"
  ),
  `p-value` = c(
    round(ece.test(X_mat, type = "bs.multiplier")$p.value, 3),
    round(ece.test(X_mat, type = "bs.parametric.lag1.diag.psd")$p.value, 3),
    round(ece.test(X_mat, type = "bs.parametric.naive")$p.value, 3),
    round(cortest.bartlett(cor(X_mat), nrow(X_mat))$p.value, 3)
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
)

kable(results, align = c("l", "c")) |>
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
```

All four tests reject the diagonal null at any conventional level. This is expected: these sectors share the same business cycle, and `NFBUS`/`BUS` in particular are near-duplicate aggregates. The Bartlett test, which does not account for the mean shifts, rejects most strongly of all — consistent with naive Pearson correlation overstating the strength of evidence when the mean is non-stationary.

---

Where this leaves us: naive Pearson correlation finds every pair significant except `NDUR`-`NFC`. ECE and oracle segmentation agree with each other almost exactly, and both find only three pairs significant: `NFBUS`-`BUS` (expected, they're near-duplicate aggregates), and `NDUR` with each of `NFBUS` and `BUS`. Every other pair — including `DUR` with anything — loses significance once the mean shift is removed. This is the mean-shift-induced spurious correlation the ECE test is designed to guard against: naive Pearson correlation on non-stationary series overstates how many sectors move together, and the diagonal tests above confirm classical methods reject the "no correlation" null much more confidently than the mean-shift-aware ones.
